clue.text: Dependable pudding — and its eating?

blocks.note: a fool is a pudding of fruit folded into cream
'the proof of the pudding is in the eating'

explanation.surface: A cook wonders whether the pudding can be trusted, and whether eating it settles the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the proof of the pudding is in the eating' lets 'its eating' stand for PROOF; the pudding is a fool, a British fruit-and-cream dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a foolproof method cannot go wrong even in careless hands, so it can be depended on.

clue.text: Duke crossing river before all others

indicators.note: to cross something is to lie across it, so the fist straddles the river and holds it in its middle

blocks.note: 'put up your dukes': dukes are fists

explanation.surface: A duke on his travels fords a river ahead of everyone else in his party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duke' reads as a nobleman; it is slang for a fist, from boxing's 'put up your dukes'.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverbial phrase for an adverb: to go first is to go before all others in order or time.

clue.text: Eggs parasites laid outside high chief’s chamber

indicators.note: the lice are laid on the outside of OFF, so they wrap round it

explanation.surface: A grim scene of insect eggs deposited around a senior figure's room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High' as in meat or game past its best means OFF; the chief is the US President, whose office is oval.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the chief is the US President, and his working room in the White House is the Oval Office.

clue.text: Is it Manx cat sitting atop monument?

indicators.note: a Manx cat has no tail, so the cat loses its last letter
in a down answer, PANTHE sits above ON

explanation.surface: Someone spots a cat perched on top of a statue and wonders if it is the tailless Isle of Man breed.
explanation.walkthrough: Manx cats, from the Isle of Man, are born without tails, so 'Manx' is a neat instruction to drop the last letter of the cat.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Pantheon in Paris is a building that honours the illustrious dead, a national monument.

clue.text: Doomed Antarctic explorer fed on exceptionally large seals?

indicators.note: to seal something is to close it in, so OS closes round ATE

explanation.surface: A polar explorer survives by eating enormous seals.
explanation.walkthrough: Seals are what Antarctic explorers really ate, so the word hides its job as a container. Captain Oates walked out of Scott's tent to his death in 1912.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: Lawrence Oates died on Scott's return from the South Pole, walking out into a blizzard.

clue.text: Lunch for example comes before tea in pecking order

blocks.note: lunch is an example of food

explanation.surface: In the order of the day's meals, lunch comes before tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a British daily timetable, where tea is an afternoon meal; 'pecking order' then turns out to be the hierarchy of who eats whom.
explanation.definitionFit: A witty literal reading: a food chain ranks animals by who eats whom, a pecking order in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Keen servant to cross stone wall once confining him?

definitions.note: the definition describes the answer by the Berlin Wall that enclosed him

indicators.note: to cross something is to span it, so EAGER stretches across ST and holds it inside

explanation.surface: An eager servant tries to climb a stone wall that has kept him penned in.
explanation.walkthrough: The wall is the Berlin Wall, which penned in the citizens of the old German Democratic Republic until 1989.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the Berlin Wall kept East Germans in, so the one it once confined is an East German.

clue.text: Language Beardsley used occasionally

indicators.note: take the letters only now and then: every other one

explanation.surface: A remark that the artist Aubrey Beardsley sometimes spoke a particular language.
explanation.walkthrough: Erse is an old name for Scottish or Irish Gaelic.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Erse, an old word for Scottish or Irish Gaelic, is one particular language.

clue.text: Spit in the food?

blocks.note: reads as the verb, spitting in disgust; it is the noun, a roasting rod
a small spit that is pushed into the food itself

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a cook has spat into a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spit' looks like the verb of disgust; it is the noun, a rod for roasting, and a skewer is a small one pushed into food.
explanation.definitionFit: A skewer is a small spit, a pointed rod that is pushed through pieces of food to cook them.

clue.text: Muscle: too much shown by English-American gladiator?

blocks.note: Maximus, hero of the film Gladiator

explanation.surface: A muscle-bound Anglo-American fighter shows off rather too much brawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Maximus is Russell Crowe's character in the film Gladiator; the question mark admits he is one gladiator standing for all.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the gluteus maximus, the big buttock muscle, is one particular muscle.

clue.text: Special occasion when message arrives from China?

definitions.text: Special occasion when message arrives from China?

blocks.note: the straight sense: a memorable, happy day
Communist China is 'Red' China, so a message from there is a letter of that colour

explanation.surface: A happy day marked by a letter from China.
explanation.walkthrough: A letter from Communist China would be a 'red letter', and the day it arrives a red-letter day; the real sense is a day marked in red on a calendar.
explanation.definitionFit: Saints' days were once printed in red in church calendars, so a red-letter day is a special occasion.

clue.text: Flying home, atmosphere foul

explanation.surface: A traveller flies back home and finds the mood there sour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flying home' reads as a journey; it is a noun phrase, the home of flying aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic gloss: an airbase is where military aircraft are kept, a home for flying machines.

clue.text: Randomly select a man to freshen up the carpets?

indicators.note: the letters are picked out in no particular order

explanation.surface: Pick any man at all to clean the carpets.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that carpets are just one thing you might steam-clean.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: carpets are the thing most often steam-cleaned, which revives them with hot vapour.

clue.text: Small turtle eschewing soft ground

blocks.note: a terrapin is a small freshwater turtle

explanation.surface: A little turtle avoids muddy ground.

explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: terrain is a stretch of land considered for its surface, the ground underfoot.

clue.text: Beginning to think, philosopher provides clothing collection

indicators.note: take the first letter of 'think'

explanation.surface: A philosopher starts thinking about clothes and supplies a wardrobe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to think' sounds like a philosopher's first stirrings, which is exactly why it hides a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A trousseau is the collection of clothes and linen a bride gathers for her marriage.

clue.text: Oceanid trapping men in the underworld

blocks.note: Dis, the Roman underworld and its god

explanation.surface: A sea nymph holds men captive in Hades.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oceanids were the daughters of Oceanus in Greek myth, and Doris was one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Doris was an Oceanid, a sea nymph and mother of the Nereids.

clue.text: Writer’s point supportive of saint, nevertheless

indicators.note: in a down answer, N goes underneath, holding up the rest

explanation.walkthrough: The definition includes the ''s', read as 'Writer is'; Robert Louis Stevenson wrote Treasure Island.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Robert Louis Stevenson, author of Treasure Island, is one particular writer.

clue.text: Dunce securing prize thus for science branch

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so ASS holds the other pieces inside

explanation.walkthrough: SIC is the Latin 'thus', printed after a quoted error to show it is as written.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: astrophysics, the physics of stars and space, is one branch of science.

clue.text: One breaking promise backed goddess to bring new life

indicators.note: the word is turned back to front

blocks.note: Ate, Greek goddess of folly and ruin

explanation.surface: Someone who broke a vow gets behind a goddess of rebirth.
explanation.walkthrough: Ate is a crossword regular: the Greek goddess of rash folly.
explanation.definitionFit: From the Latin for 'born again': to regenerate a tissue or a town is to revive it.

clue.text: ARP signal everyone understood

explanation.surface: A wartime warden's signal that everybody got.
explanation.walkthrough: ARP was Air Raid Precautions, Britain's wartime civil defence; the all-clear siren meant the raid was over.
explanation.definitionFit: The all clear was the steady siren sounded when an air raid had ended.

clue.text: Top of the Bill?

blocks.note: reads as the headline act on a theatre poster; here, the most senior officer
the Bill, or Old Bill, is British slang for the police

explanation.surface: The headline act in a theatre programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top of the bill' is the star act; 'the Bill' (or Old Bill) is British slang for the police, whose top officer in a county force is the chief constable.
explanation.definitionFit: A chief constable heads a British police force, so is top of the Bill.

clue.text: Playing well, accompanying King’s Singers

blocks.note: a player in form is playing well

explanation.surface: A choir performs well alongside the King's Singers, the famous vocal group.
explanation.walkthrough: The King's Singers are a real British vocal group, so 'Singers' looks like part of their name. Here it is slang: to sing is to inform to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: Underworld slang: an informer 'sings' to the police, so informers are singers.

clue.text: Sewer in Main Street runs through dining-room

indicators.note: ST and R run through the middle of MESS, splitting it

blocks.note: a mess is a military dining-room

explanation.surface: A drain pipe under a high street passes beneath a dining room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' reads as a drain; it is one who sews. 'Main Street' splits too: the main is the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A seamstress is a woman who sews for a living, so a sewer in the stitching sense.

clue.text: Respect sappers guarding position, so to speak

explanation.walkthrough: Sappers are military engineers, the Royal Engineers in the British army.

clue.text: Female relative, super-polite, concealing enmity at first

take the first letter of 'enmity'

clue.text: Influence result

blocks.note: the power to produce change in someone or something

clue.text: Puzzle concerned with public transport

clue.text: Socialise with ugly Romeo, cavorting in irreverent manner
